description:
Observed in examples/monte_carlo_rtp.exs (defk-9p6.17): at 1M spins, 48 Task.async_stream tasks each running a ~0.7 ms kernel ran on only 2-3 of 12 schedulers (recorded with :erlang.system_info(:scheduler_id) inside each task), while the same tasks running the Elixir model spread across all 12. That is why the 1M point of the sweep shows ~1x and the crossover is 10M, although the per-spin kernel is 3x faster.

Investigate whether this is BEAM scheduler placement for short-lived tasks whose work is one NIF call (the calling process rarely yields, so work stealing has little to steal; a kernel yields every 250 us, which at 0.7 ms per task is 2-3 yields), or an artifact of Task.async_stream's ordered chunking. Compare: tasks started with spawn_link on explicit schedulers (`:erlang.spawn_opt(..., scheduler: n)` is not available; use `Task.async_stream` with `max_concurrency: 12` and longer tasks, or batch spins per task so each call is ~10 ms), and record the scheduler spread. If placement is the cause, the catalog guidance is "give each kernel call enough work (>= a few ms) or batch", and examples/README.md gets a sentence; if there is a runtime lever (e.g. a kernel call that yields immediately once to let the scheduler balance, or `enif_schedule_nif` placement), file it as a runtime ticket.

Done when: the cause is identified with a measurement and either the README sentence or a runtime ticket exists.

comments.text: Second repro from defk-9p6.11 (examples/batched_levenshtein.exs, under load): 12 Task.async_stream tasks each calling Lev.Kernels.lev_myers on ~20k words (~0.5 ms per call) ran on schedulers 1-2 only (:erlang.system_info(:scheduler_id) before and after the call), 3.6-4.7 ms total vs 5.6 ms for the 12 calls in sequence; the same split running Elixir spread over 10-12 schedulers. :erlang.yield() before the call: still 2 schedulers; Process.sleep(1) before it: 4. This makes the batched Levenshtein verdict poor (Elixir chunks 3.8-4.2 ms vs defk chunks 4.3-4.6 ms) although the kernel is 2.4-2.8x in one process.

Cause found, measured (ALL NUMBERS UNDER LOAD: HLL and Gorilla agents benchmarking, load avg 5-7 on 12 cores; OTP 29.0.3, 12 schedulers; treatments interleaved in one VM, repeated, medians).

Mechanism: ERTS wakes a sleeping scheduler from wakeup_other_check() (erl_process.c, default +sws): each schedule() on a run queue with waiters adds left_len * reductions-of-last-run + 400, and wakes one scheduler past the +swt limit (medium 40000). defk does call enif_consume_timeslice, correctly from its clock: 100% (4000 reds) per DEFK_SLICE_US = 250 us. Elixir burns 4000 reds in ~5 us. Measured: a 0.69 ms kernel call = 9.6k reds, 2 context switches; 0.72 ms of Elixir = 597k reds, ~150 context switches (~50x more reductions per ms). So a crowded run queue under kernels takes ~50x longer to wake helpers, and tasks spawned by one process stay on its scheduler plus 1-3.

Synthetic (count_primes vs Elixir prime count of EQUAL duration, 48 tasks x 0.65 ms unless noted; wall ms median / schedulers seen):
  Task.async_stream (ordered or not): kernel 15-18 ms / 3; Elixir 4.6-6.8 / 12
  plain spawn, all 48 at once: kernel 7.1 / 11; Elixir 6.5 / 11
  Task.async + await_many: kernel 6.7 / 11; Elixir 6.3 / 11
  spawn_opt [{:scheduler, n}] (works on OTP 29, undocumented): kernel 7.2 / 12; Elixir 6.6 / 12
  +swt very_low: kernel 5.3-6.1 / 11-12; low: 6.9-7.8 / 9; very_high: 29-30 / 2 (Elixir 5.3-6.6 throughout)
  +sbwt none / very_long, +sws legacy: no change (kernel 14-18 / 3)
  DEFK_SLICE_US 100: 8.3-8.8 / 7; 50: 5.8-7.4 / 12 (dose-response). Cost on one scheduler vs yield:false: 250us +3-5%, 100us +1-12%, 50us +11-18% -> not adopted.
  simulated yield on entry (bump_reductions(4000) + yield before the call): 12-13 ms / 4 (small gain)
  10 ms calls (48 tasks): kernel 59-65 ms / 12, Elixir 61-63 / 12 -> long calls spread
  12 tasks x 0.55 ms: kernel 4.5-4.8 / 2-3, Elixir 2.0-2.4 / 8-9 (noisy)

Examples' parallel paths, default vs +swt very_low (busy schedulers = scheduler_wall_time active >= 100 us):
  monte_carlo_rtp 1M, 48 chunks: defk 16.7 ms / 4 -> 7.7 / 11; Elixir 25.8 / 11 -> 26.8 / 11
  monte_carlo_rtp 1M, 12 chunks: defk 10.2 / 7 -> 9.3 / 11
  monte_carlo_rtp 10M, 48 chunks (~5-7 ms each): defk 64 / 11 (already spreads)
  batched_levenshtein 234k, 12 chunks: defk 5.1-5.6 / 2 -> 2.3-2.5 / 11-12; Elixir 5.4 / 12 -> 4.9-5.8 / 12; one call 7.5-8.5
  cosine_topk 100k, 12 chunks: defk 11.7 / 8 -> 7.7-9.2 / 8-10; Elixir 123-134 -> 122-127 (this session's one call was 48 ms, machine heavily loaded)

Outcome: no small, clearly correct runtime fix (the slice is the only reduction-rate lever and it costs 11-18% per call). Runtime ticket defk-6lr (needs-triage) lists the levers: a placement helper using {:scheduler, n}, an adaptive slice, documenting +swt very_low. examples/README.md "Measuring correctly" item 7 gives the guidance: give each parallel kernel call a few ms of work or use fewer, bigger chunks; +swt very_low as the flag; report verdicts on a default VM. Note for the verdicts: with +swt very_low batched_levenshtein's chunks are ~2x faster than Elixir's.

title: Short kernel tasks under Task.async_stream run on only 2-3 of 12 schedulers
